image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |
raw_comment: You are leaving out an entire half of our system. You are missing how the senate relates to the house of representatives. While yes, smaller states have more power in the senate, larger states have more power in the house of representatives. This is because we have a bicameral house that favors both smaller states and larger states. If you were to effectively remove the smaller states power and base vote power off of population in the senate, you might as well have just one house of representatives. It would mess up the balance of power and smaller states would have no choice but to do what the larger states ask. Rather this bicameral system finds the best of both worlds by making sure both population and small states both agree on a bill before passing it. No change is needed.

1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

|---|---|---|

| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).

   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

I first noticed that the graph is showing what one voter in Wyoming is worth in other states in terms of voting power. When looking at the data more closely, I can see that California compared to Connecticut, Alabama, and Michigan has a much smaller percentage of black voters. I also noticed that while in all the other states, white voters make up the majority, in California the majority is made up of Hispanic voters.

Why are black people not as represented in California compared to some of the other states shown?
Why don’t states have more of an equal representation of ethnicities rather than being majorly white? Or in California’s case, majorly Hispanic.

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because everyone has somewhat of a say in terms of what happens, for example, electing government officials. So this graph gives insight into how much power someone’s vote has when compared to other states.

Headline

How Powerful is Your Vote?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
While white people are the primary voters in the other states, I noted that in California, more Hispanic voters turned out than white voters. This, in my opinion, is related to geography, immigration, and the political leanings of the state. There are numerous contributing factors, but of all the states represented, California has the greatest diversity.

What do you wonder?
I'm curious to know if immigration contributes to the ethnic variety in states like Michigan and California. Minorities vote in certain states, but not many. Being an American citizen is a requirement to vote, which is regrettably out of reach for many immigrants.

How does this relate to you and your community?
Because I am a member of the Hispanic community, one of the minority groups that is allowed to vote, this affects my community and me. If they had citizenship, I believe more Hispanics would cast ballots. I am aware of this because I live in a predominantly Hispanic neighborhood and know that some Hispanic residents want to be more active but are constrained.

What’s going on in this graph?
Does it matter if you vote?

1. **Chart type**:

   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

raw_comment:
I observe that the number of representatives varies depending on the size of the state. For instance, Michigan is a smaller state with only 18 voters, whereas California is a major state with 59 voters. The graph demonstrates how 1 voter in Wyoming has a representation that is comparable to 59 voters in California; this demonstrates that due to Wyoming being a much smaller state, the weight of a singular vote is much heavier than one in California. Additionally, it shows that white voters and representation outnumber all other races, with the exception of California, which has a higher proportion of Hispanic voters than White.
Do the state's political views change as a result of the majority of voters being white? What accounts for the majority-white representation of most states and the severe lack of minority populations? Would the graph be comparable if it had been created 10 years ago?

Voting is crucial if we want to have our voices heard in our government, and as a citizen who lives in a region with a high Hispanic population, I believe it is especially important for minorities to be represented. Diversity is necessary for us to move forward as a country and to mend fences on all sides.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |

raw_comment: According to the graph, I notice that one vote in the Senate is the same as six voters in the senate because no matter the size of the state every vote is equal in value. However, I do wonder why this is considering the fact that different states have much bigger populations than Wyoming which you would think would give it more voting power. This graph is similar to my community. In my neighborhood, there is a board that in this case represents the Senate. Each person on that board has a vote that counts as one. The size difference here can be used as the longer the person has lived in my community. It doesn't matter how long they have lived there, they will have the same vote as everyone else. This graph is showing how size does not matter. No matter how big some states are compared to others the power each one has will be the same. This rule was created back in the 1700s when America became its own country and that's how it has been run since. Each state has the same amount of power as all the others. A catchphrase for this graph would be "Size does not Matter, For evreyone is Equal"

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   Pictogram / unit chart (icon array) with grouped colored rectangles representing voters.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - Uses **small multiple grouped panels by state** (Wyoming, North Dakota, Connecticut, Alabama, Michigan, California).  
   - Within each state panel, units are **grouped by race/ethnicity category** and distinguished by **color**.  
   - The panels are arranged as **comparative examples** connected by text (“has similar representation as” / “or”), not by axes.  
   - No stacking on a common axis; units are laid out in compact grids.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| State | Categorical/nominal | Grouping into separate labeled panels; text labels |
| Number of voters / voter count | Quantitative | Number of repeated rectangular unit marks in each state panel; also stated in text labels (“1 voter”, “6 voters”, etc.) |
| Race/ethnicity (White, Black, Asian, Hispanic, Other) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue of unit marks; category labels above groups |
| Senate representation equivalence | Categorical/relational text | Text annotations connecting state examples (“has similar representation as”, “or”) |
